newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian local vote tests tense government alliance.
newsitem.headline: Italian local vote tests tense government alliance.

text.p: Voters in more than 80 cities and provinces went back to the polls on Sunday for the second round of local elections which are seen as a major test for Prime Minister Romano Prodi and his centre-left government.
The main prizes on offer are the wealthy northern cities of Milan, Turin and Trieste -- the power houses of Italian industry which have suffered in recent months of economic stagnation.

In all three cities, candidates from the ruling Olive Tree coalition face possible defeat at the hands of Silvio Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance of centre-right parties, which has been re-animated by the election contest.

First round ballots two weeks ago showed the left and right blocs evenly balanced on a national basis a year after Prodi swept to power in a surprise general election win. However the Freedom Alliance has inched ahead in a number of large cities.

The vote also revealed a collapse in support for the separatist Northern League party but growing popularity for the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures the Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament.

Some 5.43 million Italians are eligible to vote in Sunday's contest for 77 mayors and five provincial presidents between the two front runners in places where no-one gained more than 50 percent support first time around.
All eyes are fixed on the big battles in the north.
"If the Olive Tree loses Turin, Trieste and Milan then it will have lost these spring elections," La Repubblica newspaper said in an editorial on Sunday.
Of the three cities, only the Olive Tree candidate in Turin, current mayor Valentino Castellani, has signed an electoral pact with Communist Refoundation.
In Milan and Trieste, the centre-left did not want to be associated with Refoundation's brand of Marxist socialism.
Corriere della Sera newspaper said that the opposition would get a perverse boost if the Olive Tree left took Turin thanks to the hard-left, but lost elesewhere.
"It would be proof that the Olive Tree is ever more dependent on the neo-Communists," it said in an editorial.
"They could then dig in their heels over forthcoming welfare reform, and undermine still further, from the inside, the already fragile equilibrium of the governing majority," it said.

The government plans to launch a review of the welfare state next week and is looking to cut spending on pensions as it desperately fights to balance state books in time for the planned launch of the single European currency in 1999.

Refoundation is opposed to any cuts in pension benefits and the Freedom Alliance, adopting a new, tough tone in the light of its advances in the first round local vote, is unlikely to ride to Prodi's rescue in parliament, even if Europe is at stake.

The big unknown in Sunday's elections, is how supporters of the Northern League, which is pushing for the break-up of Italy, will vote. Party leader Umberto Boosi urged League sympathisers to go to the mountains for the day, but if they spurn his advice, their votes could prove decisive.

The secessionist question leapt to the top of the political agenda on Friday when eight separatists briefly occupied St Mark's Square in Venice in a bizarre bid for an independent state in the lagoon city.
Both the Olive Tree and Freedom Alliance are deeply opposed to any talk of secession but are in favour of more federalism.
